business_model: Crowdsourced personal-shopper delivery marketplace, no owned warehouse/logistics infrastructure

historical_evidence.company: Founded by Apoorva Mehta (a former Amazon supply-chain engineer), offering same-day grocery delivery via a crowdsourced network of independent 'Personal Shoppers.'
historical_evidence.market: Large, well-understood grocery-delivery market with a notable prior failure precedent (Webvan's dot-com-era collapse from over-investment in owned warehouse/logistics infrastructure) — a real, contemporaneously-known cautionary comparison.
historical_evidence.team: Founder had relevant supply-chain domain background from Amazon; Sequoia's Michael Moritz, a former Webvan board member, personally joined Instacart's board as part of the round — a notable signal given his direct historical experience with the category's most famous failure.
historical_evidence.product: App-based grocery ordering with delivery in as little as one hour, differentiated from Webvan's model specifically by using crowdsourced shoppers' own vehicles rather than owned trucks/warehouses, directly addressing the capital-intensity problem that sank the prior generation of grocery-delivery startups.
historical_evidence.execution: Raised $8.5M in Series A funding in July 2013, led by Sequoia Capital with participation from Khosla Ventures, Canaan Partners, SVAngel, and Paul Buchheit — a credible, well-regarded syndicate for a company at this stage.
historical_evidence.traction: Operating in San Francisco at the snapshot date with a stated goal of expanding to at least 10 major U.S. cities by the end of 2014; no specific order-volume or revenue figures were found in the sources reviewed.
historical_evidence.financial: The crowdsourced, asset-light delivery model was explicitly, contemporaneously framed (by the company and covering press) as structurally more capital-efficient than the owned-fleet model that had failed for Webvan — a real, articulable financial-health-relevant thesis, though not yet proven at scale as of this small Series A.
